note:
The 'who' slot accepted "Time", which reads as nonsense here — an abstract mass noun can't hold or lose currency, so "Time loses ... dollars" is grammatical but not something anyone would say. Where 3 (slot_not_category(who, 'non_quantity_holder')) is clearly meant to catch exactly this, so the gap looks like a lexicon issue rather than a rule issue: 'time' isn't a member of non_quantity_holder and should be (along with similar abstract/temporal nouns). Fix the membership and this specimen stops being generated.

Secondary, lower confidence: "loses ... seventeen sevenths more dollars" also sits oddly. 'lose' is treated as polarity-neutral in directional_change_verb, which lets it combine with dir='more' (+1). With the optional 'than X' comparison realized ("loses 20% more dollars than Tom") that's fine, but bare, without a comparison target, the decrease sense of 'lose' fights 'more'. Might be worth requiring the comparative PP when verb is 'lose'/'gain' rather than 'have'. Also, "seventeen sevenths" (2.43) as the proportional delta is legal but reads much less naturally than the "20%" form in the premise description — not marking it as a defect, just noting the fraction realizations are the awkward ones.

The premise match itself and the emitted PercentChange fact are structurally correct given the bindings; the problem is purely that the binding for 'who' should never have been allowed.

note:
Three things wrong here, and they compound.

1. item2 bound 'times' to the count noun 'time'. In an "as many ___" frame that is the worst possible filler: every English reader parses "triple as many times" as frequency, not as a count of objects. 'time'/'times' should be excluded from the item slots in the times-as-many family, the same way many_incompatible_noun already excludes others - where 7 passed precisely because 'time' is missing from that category.

2. "The money had 20 friends" is nonsense. who='money' cleared non_quantity_holder, but money is not the kind of thing that has friends. Same shape of gap as the 'Time loses ... dollars' specimen I reviewed earlier, so the who slot is letting through abstract/mass nouns generally.

3. The emitted Quantity fact is wrong as a result: {entity: money, measure: time, value: 60}. Nothing in the sentence means 60 units of time; 60 is 20 friends x 3 carried onto the wrong measure. Even if you accept the sentence, this fact should not be emitted in this form.

Minor: 'triple' in "triple as many" is not idiomatic - English wants "three times as many" there. 'triple' works as a determiner ('triple the number'), not in the as-many comparative.
sentence: The money had 20 friends and triple as many times.

note:
The arithmetic is right - Relation{factor: 2, offset: -14, subject: fia, standard: cato} is exactly what the sentence is trying to say - but the surface English does not hold up, and it fails in the frame rather than in one slot.

"14 fewer than double as much as Cato" mixes the count comparative with the mass comparative. 'fewer' selects a countable item; 'as much' is the mass frame. English forces 'less' here, which is what the rule's own model sentence uses ("250 dollars less than twice as much as Ana"). Nothing appears to tie the count/mass class of dir to the 'as much' frame, so this looks like a missing cross-slot constraint rather than a bad lexicon entry - 'fewer' is a perfectly good quantity_delta, just not in this family.

Second, 'double' does not work prenominally in a comparative: "double as much as" is not English, "twice as much as" is. 'double' is fine as a determiner ('double the amount') or a verb, so the multiplier slot needs to distinguish the two.

The flagged deficiency ('14' needs a quantifier) is the same problem seen from the other side: the elided-item variant leaves a bare numeral with no measure, so there is nothing for 'fewer' to count. Worth deciding whether this family should require an explicit measure noun on n.

note:
"Remainder were times." is not a sentence anyone would write, and there are two separate reasons.

Agreement/determiner: the model form is "The rest are dogs". Here r realized as the bare singular 'Remainder' with no determiner, then took the plural copula 'were'. Both halves are wrong - 'remainder' needs 'the' in subject position, and singular 'remainder' does not take 'were'. 'rest' gets away with the bare-ish reading that 'remainder' does not, so the remnant category is treating two nouns as interchangeable when they are not.

Lexical: attr bound to 'times' (noun 'time') again. That is the third specimen in this batch where 'time'/'times' has slipped into a count/member slot, and it never reads as a count noun - "were times" parses as frequency or as an idiom, not as membership. I would exclude 'time' from membership_member_noun and from the item slots generally; it is doing a lot of damage across rules.

The PartitionQuantity fact inherits the problem (attribute: time, value: 0), but I do not think the fact machinery is at fault - fix the two slots and the fact is fine.

note:
"John travels to eighteen fifths the amount of rabbits that plum traveled to." - the frame is right but almost every filler is wrong.

The clearest, most fixable one: frame='amount' with a count item ('rabbits'). English requires 'the number of rabbits'; 'the amount of' selects mass nouns. The rule's own model sentences both use 'the number of' with count nouns. Nothing seems to tie the frame quantifier to the countability of item, so this is a missing cross-slot constraint - and it will keep firing on every count item until it is added.

std bound to 'plum'. A plum does not travel, and it arrives lowercased in a position the reader expects a name, so the sentence reads as a typo. where 10 (slot_not_category(std, 'non_quantity_holder')) passed, so the same non_quantity_holder gap that let 'Time' and 'money' through is letting a fruit through as an agent.

'travels to rabbits' is the third problem: item sits in a destination-preposition frame, so it needs to be something you can travel to. 'countries' works in the model sentence for that reason; rabbits do not.

Smaller points, not marked: factor 3.6 (eighteen fifths) in a rule described as a pure-fraction relation is odd - I would expect proper fractions only. And the flagged deficiency ('to' needs an object) looks like a false positive to me: the stranded 'to' in "that plum traveled to" is exactly the model construction, so I would check the resolver before treating it as real.

note:
This is the most useful failure in the batch so far, because the generator and the reader disagree with each other.

The generator spent 64 attempts and emitted "There were 30 times." targeting existential-premise-bare, and then the target rule came back ABSENT - no premise rule matched, no surviving facts, and the reader reports 'were' has no subject. So the pipeline produced a sentence its own matcher cannot read.

The cause is the same 'time' problem I have now flagged four times: item bound to the count noun 'time', realized as "30 times". Every English parser, human or otherwise, takes "30 times" as a frequency adverbial, not as 30 countable objects - which is exactly why the subject disappeared and the existential reading collapsed. "There were 30 chairs" (the model) works; "There were 30 times" cannot.

Marking 'intended rule did not fire' and 'generator realization defect' together deliberately: the rule itself looks fine, it is the filler choice that broke the round trip. If 'time' is excluded from counted-item slots, I would expect this specimen class to disappear and the 64-attempt thrash to go with it.

note:
k='once' kills this one. "once as many roses" is not English - the as-many comparative takes 'twice', 'three times', 'half', but never 'once'. 'once' is a frequency adverb ('I saw it once'), and the fact that it carries multiplier value 1 in the lexicon is what let it into the k slot. Two things follow from that:

1. 'once' should not be a member of whatever multiplier category feeds this frame, regardless of its numeric value.
2. Even with a well-formed word, factor 1 is a degenerate comparison. English does not say "one times as many roses" either - at factor 1 the multiplier is dropped entirely ("as many roses as"). I would guard the frame against k=1 as well, otherwise the same shape will come back via any other unit multiplier.

The elided-standard machinery itself looks right: Relation{standard: $elided:standards$, factor: 1, measure: rose} is the correct shape for the construction, the 'with the remainder' PP resolved cleanly through quantity_remainder_preposition, and there are no collisions. This is a single bad filler, not a broken rule.

Not marking it, but 'The bird buys...' is another agent-plausibility case - birds do not buy things. Consistent with the who-slot looseness I have flagged on other specimens.

note:
Valid. "Fia was 4 years younger." is exactly the shape this rule exists to catch - a postfix comparative with no 'than Y' anchor - and it is perfectly natural English; you would read it in any narrative paragraph.

The important thing is that it emitted no facts, which is the correct behaviour here rather than an omission. The rule's job is to consume the clause so the general SVO fold cannot misread "was 4 years younger" as a bare stated Quantity(4). It did that: the span is consumed, no surviving facts, no competing match. Declining to resolve the implicit anchor is a deliberate design choice per the rule comment, and I agree with it - guessing the previous sentence's subject would be confidently wrong more often than not.

The deficiency "'younger' (comparative) needs a standard and none was found" is correct and, I would argue, is the intended output of this rule rather than a problem: the dangling comparative genuinely has no standard in this sentence. Unlike the two resolver false positives I flagged earlier (expletive 'there', stranded 'to'), this one is real and informative - it is the signal that an anchor is missing from the discourse, not from the grammar.

Nothing to fix.

note:
"The population triple as many pounds in the tree as Bira." - 64 attempts, then ABSENT: no premise rule matched, no facts. Another round trip the pipeline could not close, and the cause is the verb slot.

The rule is "X has as many ITEM as Y", a stative equality with a fixed factor of 1. verb bound to 'triple', which is a change-of-quantity verb - it asserts a threefold increase, the exact opposite of asserting equality. Two things went wrong at once and either alone would sink it:

1. Category: where 7 (slot_not_category(verb, 'non_quantity_object_verb')) is the only guard on verb here, and it does not exclude quantity-change verbs. The as-many frame needs a possession/stative verb ('has', 'holds', 'owns'), not one that already carries a multiplier. Note 'triple' also broke a specimen in my earlier batch ("triple as many times") - it is worth auditing every slot 'triple' can reach.

2. Morphology: even granting the verb, "The population triple" is not agreeing - singular subject needs 'triples'. The bare form suggests the realizer treated 'triple' as a modifier rather than the finite verb, which is probably also why the matcher then found no clause to bind.

'pounds' as the item is fine on its own (countable coins), and 'in the tree' is grammatical if odd, so I would not touch those. Fix the verb category and I expect this rule starts realizing.
sentence: The population triple as many pounds in the tree as Bira.

Unsurprisingly the target rule then came back ABSENT with no facts, and both deficiencies are genuine rather than resolver noise: 'in' has no object and 'all' has no collection, precisely because the clause the marker should attach to is missing. note:
First MATCHED specimen in several cycles, and the arithmetic is right: Relation{subject: pencil, standard: fia, measure: pound, factor: 2, offset: 14} is exactly "14 more than double". One attempt, 17/6/14 specificity, all 14 where-clauses passed. The affine machinery is working.

The rule requires the echo verb to share the matrix verb's LEMMA and to agree with its own subject - both satisfied, where 5 and where 6 both passed - but nothing ties the two verbs to the same tense. No English speaker would mix them in a single comparison; it should be 'ate ... ate' or 'eats ... eats'. note:
"Mary triple six thirds of remainder." - ABSENT, 64 attempts. verb='triple' in bare form for the fourth time, fifth uninflected-verb specimen overall. I will not restate that case; see the as-many and goal-need reviews.

The new and worthwhile finding is f='six thirds' = 2.0 in a rule whose whole subject is a fraction OF A REMNANT. You cannot take two times the rest; a proportional part of a leftover is bounded above by the leftover itself, so f must be <= 1 here. Notably the pack already knows this idea - the fraction-delta-relation comment says 'A proportional decrease cannot exceed the whole standard quantity' - it just is not enforced on this rule. Worth checking every fraction slot in the family for the same bound, since 'six thirds', 'eighteen fifths' (seen earlier this run) and 'seventeen sevenths' are all improper fractions the generator is happily producing.

No facts, no collisions, nothing else to salvage here.

note:
"Bira wants to triple 70 pencils." This one is worth reading carefully, because it corrects something I have been saying for several cycles.

The sentence is GRAMMATICAL. It is the first 'triple' specimen in this run that is. The verb slot here declares 'bare form', which is correct after infinitival 'to', so "wants to triple" is exactly right English. My earlier reviews treated bare 'triple' as a realizer bug; that diagnosis holds for the finite-position cases (the population/the age/Mary) but not here. The realizer did the right thing this time.

The defect is purely semantic, and it is a clean example of why multiplier verbs do not belong in quantity slots. The rule states a GOAL quantity: "Lena wants to collect 30 stamps" means the target is 30. With 'triple' as the goal verb, 70 is the BASE, not the target - the sentence means Bira is aiming at 210. The counted item has switched roles.

And the consequence is visible in the surviving fact: Quantity{entity: bira, measure: pencil, value: 70, verb: want}, emitted by the fold after the target rule went ABSENT. That value is wrong. It is not merely an incomplete reading; it silently discards the multiplier and records the base as though it were the wanted amount. Second time this run the fold has produced a confidently wrong fact on a clause the targeted rule declined (the other was "Eron need 15 times"), which strengthens my earlier suggestion that the fold should be suppressed, not left to guess, when a rule that clearly owns a clause backs out.

So: exclude multiplier verbs from goal/quantity verb slots on semantic grounds, independent of the separate agreement bug.
sentence: Bira wants to triple 70 pencils.

note:
"The area triple 10 more than zero sixths as many pencils with its remainder as my friend Fia." ABSENT, 64 attempts. Bare 'triple' against a singular subject again - sixth uninflected-verb case, fifth 'triple' - already covered, not restating.

Last cycle the fraction slot produced a value ABOVE the legal range (2.0 in a fraction-of-remnant); this cycle it has produced the degenerate value at the bottom, 0. "zero sixths as many pencils" is not something anyone writes, and as an affine relation it collapses the standard term entirely - subject = 0 x standard + 10 - which means the rule is no longer expressing a relation at all, just a bare quantity. So the fraction slot needs BOTH bounds, 0 < f <= 1, not just an upper one. Two cycles, two different out-of-range fraction values, in two different rules of the same family - I would fix this at the fraction type rather than per-rule.

Also worth noting the pile-up of dangling references in one sentence: 'its remainder' and 'my friend Fia' both flagged, on top of who='the area' which cannot hold pencils. That is three separate context-dependence problems in a single specimen, where previous ones had at most one. Still not marking the possessives individually - my position on those has not changed - but at this density the sentence would be unusable even with every other defect fixed.
sentence: The area triple 10 more than zero sixths as many pencils with its remainder as my friend Fia.

The rule's own model uses "12 inches longer", a realistic figure. note:
"Apple triple eleven fifths more money." ABSENT, 64 attempts. Bare 'triple' in finite position, bare common-noun subject 'Apple'. Nothing new; see the earlier reviews.

note:
"Time dropped thrice as much." MATCHED in one attempt, and this one sharpens a recommendation I have been making since my first review, so it is worth more than its surface looks.

The sentence is structurally fine. As an anaphoric continuation - item elided, standard pointing back to an earlier quantity - it is exactly what the rule describes, and Relation{subject: time, standard: $anaphor:quantity$, factor: 3, offset: 0, verb: drop} is the right shape. The self-decline machinery worked too: both continuation sentinels stayed unbound, so the rule correctly kept the match instead of handing off.

The defect is who='Time' again. But look at the where list: number_compatible, slot_not_category(k, predeterminer_multiplier), absent(partitive), unbound(sentinels). FOUR clauses, and NOT ONE of them is slot_not_category(who, 'non_quantity_holder'). The percent-change rules have that guard (where 3), times-as-much has it (where 7), affine-frame-relation has it twice (where 9 and 10), anchored-relation-postfix-dimension has it twice (where 4 and 5). This rule simply does not.

That changes the fix. I have been saying 'add time to non_quantity_holder', and that is still necessary - but it is not sufficient, because on this rule the category is never consulted. Adding the lemma would silence the percent-change and times-as-much cases and leave this one producing 'Time dropped thrice as much' forever. The guard needs to be audited for PRESENCE across every rule whose who slot holds a quantity, not just for membership.

Marking premise-too-broad rather than wrong-category-membership for exactly that reason: the category is not wrong here, it is absent.
sentence: Time dropped thrice as much.

note:
"In 18 years Aven would be double as old as Cato." The temporal arithmetic is impeccable - Relation{factor: 2, offset: 0, subject_offset: 18, standard_offset: 18} correctly ages both parties by 18 and states the ratio at that point, which is the whole difficult part of this rule. The failure is one word: k='double'.

"double as old as" is not English. The comparative frame takes 'twice', 'three times', 'half'; 'double' works as a predeterminer ('double the amount', 'double his age') but cannot sit in an "as ADJ as" comparison. I flagged the identical shape in an earlier cycle on affine-times-as-much-elided ("double as much as").

And here is the part that matters, because it is the second consecutive cycle showing the same structural problem. The pack ALREADY HAS the right guard for this. The previous specimen I reviewed - anaphoric-multiplier-standard-as-much - carries slot_not_category(k, 'predeterminer_multiplier') as its where 2, which is precisely what would block 'double' in a comparative. This rule's where list is only three clauses long (bound_requires_type, distinct, absent(temporal_marker)) and does not include it. k is typed bare 'multiplier' and admits everything.

So, two cycles running:
- cycle 16: non_quantity_holder guard exists on five rules, missing on anaphoric-multiplier-standard-as-much, so 'Time' got through.
- cycle 17: predeterminer_multiplier guard exists on anaphoric-multiplier-standard-as-much, missing here, so 'double' got through.

The two rules each hold the guard the other one needs. That reframes the whole defect class: this is not a lexicon problem and not a rule-logic problem, it is guard COVERAGE - the right constraints exist but are applied per-rule by hand and the matrix has holes. A mechanical audit (for every rule, which of the standard slot guards apply given its slot types) would likely close more defects than any individual fix I have recommended in seventeen cycles.

Unrelated, low confidence: the two deficiencies read "I have no information about the word 'be'" and "...'old'", for tokens the rule declares as required literals. That phrasing looks like a resolver gap rather than a real finding, but it is a different message from the subject/object flags I have been calling false positives, so someone may want to check what produces it.
sentence: In 18 years Aven would be double as old as Cato.

note:
"The flower had 9 times in my tree and twice as many prices." ABSENT, 64 attempts. And this one obliges me to correct what I wrote last cycle.

Last cycle I concluded the defect class was guard COVERAGE, not the lexicon - two rules each missing the guard the other one had. This specimen is the counter-example, and it is unambiguous. This rule carries ELEVEN where-clauses and is fully guarded: slot_not_category(who, 'non_quantity_holder') at where 6, slot_not_category(k, 'predeterminer_multiplier') at where 3, AND slot_not_category(item1/item2, 'many_incompatible_noun') at where 7 and 8 - a category whose entire purpose is keeping unsuitable nouns out of "as many X" slots.

Every one of those guards PASSED. who='the flower' cleared non_quantity_holder. item1='9 times' cleared many_incompatible_noun. The guards are present and correctly written; the categories they consult are simply missing the members that matter. k='twice' is the only slot that behaved, and only because 'twice' is genuinely fine.

So the honest picture is both, not either:
- coverage holes, where a correct guard is absent from a rule that needs it (cycles 16 and 17)
- membership gaps, where the guard fires but the category is underpopulated (here)
A coverage audit alone would not have saved this specimen. Adding 'time' to many_incompatible_noun and 'flower' to non_quantity_holder would.

Also worth noting: the fold again produced a fact on the declined clause - Predication{subject: flower, verb: have, dobj: "my"}. dobj is the bare possessive determiner 'my'. That is the third fold-emitted wrong fact I have logged (after 'Eron need 15 times' and 'Bira wants to triple 70 pencils'), and it is the worst-formed of the three.

note:
"Storeroom wanted triple this many." The anaphoric machinery is fine - Relation{standard: $anaphor:quantity$, factor: 3, offset: 0} is the right shape, the demonstrative was consumed as designed, and the negative-lookahead on direct_std_seen correctly kept this short form rather than deferring. The failure is k='triple'.

"triple this many" is not English. The 'this many' pro-form takes comparative multipliers - "twice this many", "three times this many" - while 'triple' and 'double' are predeterminers that need an actual noun phrase: "triple this amount", "triple the number". What makes this worth flagging rather than shrugging at is that the rule's own comment already reasons about exactly this class of constraint: it says bare "twice many" is not English and that the pattern is literally gated on 'many' for that reason. The author has thought about which multiplier shapes the frame admits. But k is declared as bare type 'multiplier' and the four where-clauses here are number_compatible, non_quantity_holder on who, absent(partitive), and unbound(direct_std_seen). None of them constrain k at all.

So: a rule that documents an English-shape restriction on its multiplier slot, and then does not enforce one. I have marked premise-too-broad for that, and sentence-ungrammatical for the output.

Second, who='Storeroom'. It cleared non_quantity_holder, but a storeroom cannot want anything - 'want' needs an animate subject, and nothing here checks that. It is also a bare singular common noun with no determiner, saved from looking broken only by sentence-initial capitalisation, which is a realization pattern I have now seen on several packs.

The arithmetic and the anaphor resolution both worked. This is one unguarded slot and one implausible agent, not a broken rule.

note:
"John needs 1 fewer shoppers than Mary." One narrow defect, and it is a good one because it only shows up at a single value of n.

"1 fewer shoppers" is wrong. With the numeral one English takes the singular: "1 fewer shopper", "one fewer shopper than Mary". Everything above 1 is fine - "20 fewer shoppers" is exactly the rule's own model sentence. So the rule works for every value of n except one, and n=1 is precisely what the generator drew here.

The cause is visible in the slots. item is hard-typed 'plural' (the rule description calls it the explicit plural measure), n is type 'number' with no relationship to it, and the three where-clauses are number_compatible(who, need), distinct(who, std), and many_incompatible_noun on item. number_compatible is checking SUBJECT against VERB - who='John' singular, need='needs' singular - not the numeral against the noun. Nothing anywhere ties n's value to item's number.

Two ways to fix it and they are not equivalent: either add a cross-slot constraint that forces item singular when n=1, or exclude n=1 from this rule and let a singular sibling handle it. I would lean to the first, since "one fewer shopper" is a perfectly natural premise and losing it would be a real gap.

Everything else here is right. Relation{subject: john, standard: mary, measure: shopper, factor: 1, offset: -1} is the correct affine shape for a comparative need, the rule stayed properly separate from goal-need-quantity's absolute form, and 'shopper' passed many_incompatible_noun legitimately.

The deficiency "'1' (value) needs a quantifies and none was found" is, unusually, pointing at the same token as the real defect - though I read it as the resolver noting a bare numeral rather than diagnosing the agreement problem.
sentence: John needs 1 fewer shoppers than Mary.

note:
"Fia buys thirty fourths more than their gardener John." The structure is right and the arithmetic is right - f=7.5, dir='more', factor 8.5, which is 1 + 7.5 and exactly what a 750% increase means. The elided-measure shape, the appositive, the anchoring to a proper name all worked. The defect is the fraction VALUE, and I want to be careful about it because the obvious complaint is the wrong one.

This frame is genuinely idiomatic for PROPER fractions. "a third more than Ann", "two thirds more than Ann" - both perfectly natural, and close cousins of the rule's own model, "20% more than Ann". So the fraction slot is not wrong in principle. What breaks is improper fractions: "thirty fourths more than John" forces the reader to compute 30/4 = 7.5 before the sentence means anything, and no writer would ever put it that way. At that magnitude English switches construction entirely - "seven and a half times as much as John", or "750% more".

The guard is explicit that this is intentional: proportional_delta_compatible reports "allowed magnitude was unbounded increase". Decreases are correctly capped at 100% - you cannot lose more than you have - but increases have no cap, and that asymmetry is mathematically sound. The problem is that it is being applied to a slot whose SURFACE FORM only survives below 1. So I would either restrict f to proper fractions in this rule and let a times-as-much sibling carry increases above 1, or keep the range and fix realization to switch phrasing when f exceeds 1. Marking premise-too-broad for that, not the guard.

note:
"The key had nine eighths as many birds with the rest as the hamster." Two defects, and the first is a direct repeat of last cycle - which makes it evidence rather than noise.

f='nine eighths' = 1.125. Last cycle it was 'thirty fourths' = 7.5 on fraction-delta-relation-elided; this is a different rule in the same family and the same class of value. And here the mismatch is sharper, because this rule's model sentence is "Kelcie read HALF as many books as Megan". Half. The frame is built for proper fractions and reads perfectly with them; "nine eighths as many birds" makes a reader stop and divide. Two rules, two consecutive cycles, both admitting fractions above 1 into frames that only survive below it. I would treat the fraction type itself as the place to fix this rather than either rule.

Second, who='key'. A key does not have birds. This rule carries SIXTEEN where-clauses - bound_requires_type, number_compatible, five separate verb_role_compatible checks, many_incompatible_noun on item, attribute_compatible, distinct(who,std), distinct(item,std), category_nonoverlap - and not one of them is slot_not_category(who, 'non_quantity_holder'). Worth contrasting with the times-as-many-conjunct specimen I reviewed a few cycles ago, where that guard WAS present and the failure was a membership gap instead. So both halves of the pattern I logged on the previous pack survive here: guards missing from rules that need them, and guards present but under-populated. This one is the first kind, and being missing from a 16-clause rule shows it is not a matter of the rule being lightly specified.

Also worth noting, not marked: the remnant PP lands inside the comparative frame - "as many birds WITH THE REST as the hamster" - which splits 'as many X' from its 'as Y' and makes the sentence hard to parse even once the fillers are sane. If that optional branch is going to attach here it probably belongs after the standard.

The arithmetic is right: Relation{factor: 1.125, offset: 0} is exactly 9/8.

It says trailing_adv is "scoped to the pre-existing `adverb` sense (structural, no word list)" - an explicit design decision to avoid enumerating words. This specimen is what that decision costs: 'off' is a perfectly good adverb, so the type check passes, and "and off had 20 eggs" comes out. The position only accepts a narrow temporal/aspectual set - 'currently' (the model's own choice), 'now', 'still'. Structural scoping cannot distinguish those from 'off', 'away', 'quietly'. I do not think this is fixable without either a word list or a narrower declared category, and the rule already assumes it is skippable, so a bare "...and had 20 eggs" would be the safer default realization.

note:
"The sticker teaches seventy ninths as many balls in my storeroom." The elided-standard machinery worked - $elided:standard$ is correctly reserved as the sentinel, where 8 (unbound(std_seen)) held so the rule did not wrongly claim a clause with an explicit "as Y" continuation, and the location PP resolved cleanly through quantity_location_preposition. Two things sink it.

f='seventy ninths' = 7.78. This frame is idiomatic for proper fractions - the rule's own model uses "half as many blue ones" - and collapses above 1. "seventy ninths as many balls" forces the reader to divide 70 by 9 before the sentence means anything, and at that magnitude English abandons the construction entirely for "nearly eight times as many". I have now seen this same class of value on fraction slots in two other packs, so I would fix it at the fraction type - bound it to (0, 1] wherever the surface form is an 'as many' or 'more than' comparative - rather than rule by rule.

Second, the who/verb/item triple is incoherent in two directions at once. A sticker cannot teach, and nobody teaches balls. where 5 checks who against non_quantity_holder and 'sticker' passed it, so that is a membership gap. But the deeper problem is that nothing relates the verb to its object: 'teach' takes a subject that can instruct and an object that can be taught, and neither constraint exists here. item passed only many_incompatible_noun, which is about countability, not aboutness.

One small positive worth recording: the fact's verb field carries "teach", the lemma, even though the surface form is 'teaches'. That is the opposite of what I saw twice in the gsm8k pack, where the field held the inflected form. Different pack, so not a contradiction - but if the two packs are meant to share fact schemas, this one is doing it the way I would expect and that is a useful reference point.

'my' with no referent is the usual isolated-specimen artefact; not marking it.
sentence: The sticker teaches seventy ninths as many balls in my storeroom.

note:
"The bench takes 2 trees more than your teacher Dena." Grammatical, correctly shaped, correct fact - Relation{measure: tree, factor: 1, offset: 2, verb: take} with the postfix count-comparative order the rule describes. The problem is that a bench cannot take anything.

What makes this one worth reading is HOW the bench got in, because this rule is better guarded than most I have seen and still admitted it. The who slot does not merely exclude a bad category - it POSITIVELY requires membership: "common nouns in category 'quantity_holder'". That is a stronger design than the non_quantity_holder exclusion used elsewhere, and I want it on record as the better pattern.

It still failed, via the taxonomy: 'bench' satisfied it through bench -> quantity_location -> quantity_holder. So locations are modelled as quantity holders, which is defensible for stative readings ("there are 3 books on the bench") but wrong the moment the verb is agentive. Holding a quantity and ACTING on one are different capabilities, and quantity_holder currently conflates them. That is the fix I would make: split the stative holder sense from the agentive one, or require an animate subject when the verb is agentive.

Second, and consistent with something I saw in the other pack today: where 7 is a verb_role_compatible check that would relate the verb to its object, and it passed VACUOUSLY - "verb='take' was outside triggering category 'shucking_verb'". These role checks only engage for verbs that are categorised, so an uncategorised verb silently disables them. That is the second pack in which I have watched that mechanism no-op rather than fail, and it is the same shape of miss both times.

Marking missing-cross-slot rather than wrong-category-membership deliberately: 'bench' IS legitimately a quantity_location, so its membership is not wrong. What is missing is any constraint tying an agentive verb to a subject that can act.

'your' with no referent is the usual artefact; not marking it.
sentence: The bench takes 2 trees more than your teacher Dena.

note:
"Aven ate thirty sixths more than its violinist Cato." Arithmetic correct - f=5.0, dir='more', factor 6 - and the elided-measure shape held. Two defects, one recurring and one new.

f='thirty sixths' = 5.0, so the sentence claims a 500% increase and expresses it as a fraction. This is the third specimen today, across two different packs and three different rules, where a fraction slot has produced a value above 1 in a frame that only reads naturally below it. The guard is explicit that this is intended - proportional_delta_compatible reports "allowed magnitude was unbounded increase" - and I agree the asymmetry is mathematically right, since a decrease cannot exceed 100% but an increase can. The mismatch is that the SURFACE form does not survive the range the maths permits. "a third more than Cato" is idiomatic; "thirty sixths more than Cato" makes the reader do division before the sentence means anything. Given how consistently this reproduces, I would fix it at the fraction type rather than per rule: either bound f to (0, 1] in comparative frames, or have realization switch to a times/percent construction when f exceeds 1.

The new one is appos_det='its' on a human possessor: "its violinist Cato", where the possessor is Aven, a person. English needs 'his', 'her' or 'their' there; 'its' is neuter and reads as a typo or as treating Aven as an object. This rule has only three where-clauses (bound_requires_type, proportional_delta_compatible, distinct) and none of them constrain appos_det. Worth noting that the animacy distinction is not missing from the wider system - a rule I reviewed in the other pack today declared its equivalent slot as category 'animate_possessive_determiner', which is exactly the guard needed here. So this looks like the same coverage-hole shape I have logged before: the right constraint exists somewhere in the family and is simply absent from this rule.

Not marked: 'its' also shows up as a dangling-reference deficiency, but that flag is about the missing antecedent, not the animacy error, and the animacy error is the real defect - it would still be wrong even with a referent present.
sentence: Aven ate thirty sixths more than its violinist Cato.

note:
"Mary was twice that many." The anaphoric machinery is right - Relation{standard: $anaphor:quantity$, factor: 2} is the correct shape, the demonstrative was consumed, and both self-decline guards held. The defect is verb='was'.

With a copula, the sentence equates a person with a count: Mary IS twice some quantity. That is a category error, not just an odd reading - people are not numbers. The frame needs a possession or event verb: "Mary HAD twice that many" is the sentence this rule is trying to produce, and the sibling's own model ("the bird caught 8 fish... and twice this many by night") uses exactly that kind of verb.

What lets it through is the now-familiar vacuous pass. where 4 is verb_role_compatible(verb, ['who'], verb_cat='animate_subject_verb', role_cat='quantity_event_participant') - precisely the check that should relate the subject to the verb - and it reports "verb='be' was outside triggering category 'animate_subject_verb'". So it passed by not applying. This is the THIRD specimen today, across both packs and three different rules, where a verb_role_compatible guard no-opped because the verb was uncategorised. I now think this is the single most systematic weakness I have seen in this project: the mechanism is well designed but fails open, so every verb missing from the triggering categories silently disables the agent/object check that depends on it. Failing closed, or at minimum reporting uncategorised verbs as a coverage gap, would turn three separate specimen defects into one fix.

Credit where due, and it is directly relevant: this rule declares verb as "type 'verb', FINITE FORM". That is exactly the constraint whose absence produced "Pumpkin repainting 19 fewer..." in the gsm8k pack earlier today - a participle in a finite position. Here the requirement is stated explicitly and 'was' satisfies it. Different pack, so not a fix I can claim, but it is the right pattern and worth pointing at.

I have marked missing-cross-slot rather than a lexical defect because 'be' is a perfectly good finite verb; what is absent is any constraint tying THIS frame to a verb that can take a quantity as its object.
